AJK.name: Juneau
AJK.excerpt: LONG TERM.../Wednesday through Friday/... With the most impactful weather in the rear-view, winds across the panhandle begin to diminish through Wednesday.

sections.name: Synopsis
paragraphs: - Fog and Freezing fog continue for the central panhandle into this morning creating difficult travel conditions.

- A stronger low pressure system moves north into the southeastern Gulf of Alaska Monday, increasing winds across the southern inner channels and the offshore Gulf of Alaska coastal waters into Tuesday.
- An associated front with the Gulf of Alaska low pressure system moves into the southern Panhandle Monday increasing rain chances Monday into Tuesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: / through Sunday night / A low south of the gulf of Alaska will be rotating a band of rain and wind north into the southeast gulf and into the panhandle then starting north through the panhandle. Wind gusts to 40 to 45 mph for the coastal communities. Gusts mostly for the Prince of Wales Island and possibly Metlakatla region to Tuesday morning. Chances of rain to start then to Categorical overnight and into the start of Tuesday, Snow may mixed in or be the precipitation type for the northern panhandle or north central. Accumulations are expected to be on the light side.

LONG TERM.../Wednesday through Friday/... With the most impactful weather in the rear-view, winds across the panhandle begin to diminish through Wednesday. Rain is likely to continue due to a series of fronts moving through the area, but winds are expected to diminish to less than 20kts in the inner channels, and less than 30kts in Lynn Canal, Clarence Strait, and coastal Gulf waters. A series of about 3 or 4 fronts are expected to track across the panhandle from Wednesday through Saturday night bringing light to moderate rain, but are expected to be seasonable. With low pressure moving through the gulf and high pressure established over the Yukon and British Columbia, a stronger east/west gradient sets up across the panhandle. Winds are likely to be east to northeast in direction through much of this time with east/west oriented channels likely to see channeling of winds.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: High pressure will keep temperatures warm and snow levels near 6500-7500 ft across the region on Friday and Saturday, but Pacific moisture will continue to bring pulses of precipitation despite ridging.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Light valley rain and mountain snow showers expected through this afternoon.
- Dry conditions on Tuesday with valley fog developing overnight.
- Unsettled weather will return Wednesday through the end of the week alongside warmer temps and higher snow levels.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A weak shortwave trough will move over the region this morning, bringing scattered valley rain showers and mountain snow showers. The latest hi-res models show limited additional accumulations around 1-3 inches of snow tonight in the mountains, but localized terrain enhanced showers could bring heavier accumulations in the central ID mountains. High pressure will build into the region late Monday evening, with brief warming and drying on Tuesday. A deep closed low off the PacNW Coast will push breezy southerly winds to the region today and tomorrow. Southerly winds will be highest in the Baker Valley and southern portions of Harney-Malheur County today, with increasing winds across the Snake Plain tomorrow. A weak upper level trough will then move across the region on Wednesday, bringing low chances (<20%) of precipitation across high terrain and a slight cool down. A strong upper level trough will move onshore to Washington State on Thanksgiving Day, with models coming into better agreement on the holiday pattern. Robust zonal flow aloft will effectively transport Pacific moisture across the region, with high precipitation amounts likely across the mountains in northeast Oregon and central Idaho. Breezy winds will accompany this moisture, especially on mountain ridgetops in southwest Idaho.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: High pressure will keep temperatures warm and snow levels near 6500-7500 ft across the region on Friday and Saturday, but Pacific moisture will continue to bring pulses of precipitation despite ridging. The ridge will begin to weaken on Saturday, with another closed low/upper level trough moving into the region on Sunday. This will likely bring cooler temperatures, lower snow levels, and another push of widespread precipitation to the area. Accumulations look to generally be minimal with each round of precipitation, but the length of time of this wet period will bring many sites to near record high precipitation amounts for November. Several SNOTEL sites at higher locations in the Steens, Owyhee, and Boise Mountains are recording near record snow depth for November. For example, the station at Bogus Basin measured 20 inches for the current snow depth (near 95th percentile) while the median snow depth for late November is 9 inches, more than double the typical snow depth for early winter.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Looking ahead, ensembles continue to hint at another round of mountain snow potentially arriving by Friday morning, while the plains are expected to remain dry. Temperatures will trend well above seasonal averages heading into the weekend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Patchy freezing fog possible for portions of Lincoln, Elbert, and Weld Counties Monday morning.
- A quick-hitting storm system will bring a round of mountain snow showers today, with a few light accumulations possible across the Palmer Divide and adjacent plains.
- Cooler fall temperatures will continue through Tuesday, with a gradual warming trend beginning Wednesday.
- No major travel impacts are expected during the Thanksgiving travel period.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: While minimal weather impacts are expected across the forecast area this holiday week, a few disturbances will move through the Intermountain West, bringing periodic chances for light snowfall across the mountains. Overall, relatively quiet weather is expected through the forecast period, with a gradual warming trend beginning by mid-week.

The first disturbance is still on track to move across the region later today, potentially creating some travel headaches along the high mountain passes and I-70 mountain corridor this afternoon and evening. But before it arrives, portions of Lincoln, Elbert, and Weld Counties will have to contend with some patchy freezing fog this morning, with current observations showing low stratus are already beginning to settle in. While a Dense Fog Advisory doesn't seem warranted at this time, conditions will be monitored to see how things evolve, but folks should be prepared for some patchy fog out there this morning, with the greatest impacts expected along I-70 through Elbert and Lincoln Counties.

With regards to today's storm system, while the greatest QG forcing will remain to our south, a brief period of enhanced QG ascent is expected as the shortwave tracks across the Rockies. Forecast soundings show a deeply saturated profile, with the DGZ situated within the layer of strongest lift. Additionally, lapse rates approaching 9C/km are expected for a few hours leading up to sunset, which could support the development of a few convective snow showers. Given the steep lapse rates and favorable DGZ placement, snowfall rates could briefly exceed what the broader- scale forcing might suggest. Thus, while overall snowfall accumulations are expected to remain relatively light, briefly heavier convective snow showers could create locally hazardous travel conditions, especially across mountain passes and the I-70 mountain corridor.

QPF has been trended upward to account for this potential and better align with recent guidance. Generally, expecting between 1-3 inches of snowfall along the I-70 mountain corridor and Continental Divide, although some locally higher amounts cannot be ruled out where all the ingredients come together. The remainder of the mountains should see around an inch or less, with a few tenths to a half inch expected for elevations as low as 7,500 feet. PoPs and QPF have also been extended to include the Palmer Divide and adjacent plains, where a few tenths to a tenth of an inch of snowfall are now included in the latest forecast package. Temperatures will remain below seasonal averages today and Tuesday.

Subsidence will develop Tuesday morning behind the departing system as an amplified upper-level ridge shifts eastward across the Rockies, bringing an end to snow showers and a return to warmer and drier conditions across the forecast area. Afternoon high temperatures will gradually climb through the week, with Thursday's holiday weather shaping up to be mild and dry. Highs are expected to reach the mid 50s along the urban corridor and mid 40s across the mountain valleys.

Looking ahead, ensembles continue to hint at another round of mountain snow potentially arriving by Friday morning, while the plains are expected to remain dry. Temperatures will trend well above seasonal averages heading into the weekend.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Ensemble consensus completely falls apart Saturday onwards with a remarkably large spread between extremes. The suite is just about evenly split between two highly divergent scenarios.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Chilly temperatures and mostly cloudy skies are expected Monday with areas of morning freezing fog possible.
- Elevated winds are possible Tuesday night for the wind prone areas of southeast Wyoming.
- Another round of potentially more widespread strong winds is possible Thursday night into Friday, and possibly longer.
- Significant forecast uncertainty exists for the weekend due to an unusually large range of possible forecast outcomes.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Another chilly day is on tap for the area today as a strengthening surface high pressure system nestles itself up against the mountains. Weak upslope flow over the High Plains this morning is helping to fill in low cloud cover and fog once again. As of now, this is mostly concentrated along and north of the US-20 corridor and into Platte County. With abundant mid to upper level cloud cover also rolling it, it is difficult to see the low cloud deck on satellite imagery, so trying primarily have to use webcams to ascertain its current position. High resolution model guidance shows fog and low clouds continuing to expand for much of the area along and east of I-25 over the next several hours, with a second area potentially developing over eastern Laramie county into the southern Nebraska panhandle. Temperatures are well below freezing once again, so this will come in as freezing fog in areas where the cloud deck intersects with the terrain. Fog is very patchy now, but it is possible that it becomes widespread enough in a few hours to warrant an advisory. Fog will also likely persist longer than usual this morning with little heating from above. Fog coverage may not maximize until around 8-9AM, and could hold on until 11AM or even noon in some isolated locations. Mostly cloudy skies are expected across the entire area today, though a few breaks of sunshine are expected around Laramie and Cheyenne. With the cloud cover, temperatures will struggle to warm. Highs are expected to be in the mid 30s for much of the High Plains, but the Cheyenne to Rawlins corridor may manage to reach the upper 30s to lower 40s. A weak upper level system will traverse just south of the area today. Forcing is very limited, but we may see a few light snow showers reach as far north as our southern mountains. Low end Pops were maintained here, but a dusting to an inch would be the high-end scenario. Another round of spotty fog and freezing fog is possible tonight into Tuesday morning.

The split trough will move off to the east on Tuesday as narrow ridging tries to build back in behind. With more sunshine expected and the chilly surface high retreating off to the east, areas over the High Plains should gain about 10F on Monday's highs, though Laramie and Rawlins will be similar. The northern component of the split trough will be simultaneously diving southward as the feature moves out, which will tighten the pressure gradient/low- level height gradient across the terrain barrier Tuesday into Tuesday night. Expect gusty winds to gradually increase in the typical wind prone areas through the day Tuesday, peaking Tuesday evening. Probabilities for high winds have backed off a touch with this model cycle, to around 40% for Arlington, 30% for the I-80 summit, and 20% for Bordeaux. This is mainly because recent model guidance has trended weaker with the development of a lee cyclone over the High Plains, reducing the MSLP gradient compared to previous forecasts. Low-level height gradients remain a little below what we'd like to see for a gap wind event. For now, the forecast includes gusts around the 40 to 55 mph for the gap areas.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Winds will gradually decrease Wednesday as the split trough moves away from the area. Our slow warming trend will continue, with areas along and west of I-25 jumping perhaps 3-5F from Tuesday, while the Nebraska panhandle sees similar temperatures. while a very weak vort- max will pass through the area Wednesday night, the only notable impact looks like some more cloud cover overnight. Thanksgiving day looks quite pleasant across the area, with decreasing cloud cover and temperatures returning to above seasonal averages. Look for highs in the low to mid 50s for the High Plains, and 40s around Laramie and Rawlins. Winds should be light to breezy for most of the day on Thursday, but could be increasing by the end of the day.

An interesting and challenging forecast is setting up for the Friday through Sunday period. As of now, there is medium confidence through about Friday, and then confidence completely falls apart for Saturday and Sunday with wildly different model solutions possible. To start the active period, a very powerful moisture laden Pacific jet stream is favored to surge into the Pacific northwest on Thanksgiving Day, with the nose of the jet streak encroaching on our area by the evening/overnight hours. This will be developing on the fringe of a strong, organized ridge building into the southwest US and associated with a sharp temperature gradient. Initially, we should be solidly south of the temperature gradient. This puts us in the right exit region of the jet streak, where synoptic subsidence is favored. As a result, expect winds to increase Thursday night for the wind prone areas, spreading into the Plains on Friday. LREF median 700-mb winds are around 45 to 50 knots, with several members closer to 60 knots. This is a pretty good signal for high winds at this lead time, suggesting potential for a middle-tier high wind event at least for the wind prone areas, possibly spreading into adjacent zones. For the typical gap areas, in-house guidance is quite aggressive, giving a 70%-80% probability for high winds. More likely than not, Friday will be another mild day, but there is a little bit of bust potential on forecast highs if the cold front arrives earlier than expected. The jet will also have a fair amount of deep moisture with it, increasing the chances for orographic mountain snowfall beginning Friday.

Ensemble consensus completely falls apart Saturday onwards with a remarkably large spread between extremes. The suite is just about evenly split between two highly divergent scenarios. The key piece of the puzzle is the strength of the ridge moving into the southwest CONUS. In the first scenario, the ridge is quite strong and also progresses eastward more rapidly, nudging the jet off to the north for the weekend. This would shut off the mountain-snow tap and lead to a significant warm-up for much of the area. The jet will still be close enough that even in this scenario, the potential for high winds will persist through Saturday and Sunday. The mountains would still likely see some snow, but amounts would be much lower due to the shorter duration of moist orographic ascent. Some precipitation spreading into the plains could still be possible in this scenario as the ridge lifts to the northeast (overrunning ascent) in the Friday night time frame. The other scenario involves the upper level ridge coming in slightly weaker and slower. The result keeps the jet near or even just south of our area Saturday and Sunday, pushing the temperature gradient through our area, probably around Friday night. This would continue moist orographic ascent in the mountains through Saturday and Sunday, and result in dramatically colder temperatures for the High Plains. In addition, an arctic front stalled somewhere across our area would suggest the possibility for frontogenetic and overrunning ascent, and thus higher chances for snow to spread into the plains. As far as forecast outcome, the first scenario would mean highs Saturday and Sunday in the 50s to low 60s and largely dry, while the second scenario would keep us shivering in the 20s and 30s with snow showers possible! NBM guidance is essentially an average of these two scenarios, and thus is likely to be wrong, but it's impossible to say in which direction. Therefore, it is not prudent to differ from NBM guidance significantly with models more or less evenly split. This period will need to be closely monitored in the coming days.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Skies will clear by Tuesday morning with northerly flow behind the departing trough as a high pressure ridge moves in from the west. This will lead to dry conditions and much colder temperatures Tuesday night as efficient radiational cooling takes place.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A quick-moving system will bring snow to the mountains and a rain/snow mix for the valleys today, with snowfall totals up to 2 to 5 inches.
- Active weather remains possible late Thanksgiving week, but some details still remain uncertain. Stay tuned for updates to timing and impacts as they become available.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A fast-moving trough will track across eastern Utah and western Colorado today and tonight with the trough axis pushing across the Divide during evening rush hour. Southwest flow will focus precipitation across the Four Corners with the San Juans being favored for accumulating snowfall before the low lifts across the central mountain corridor with some wraparound precipitation possible over the central mountains tonight. A rain/snow mix is expected over the valleys, becoming all rain as temperatures warm throughout the day. Steep lapse rates this afternoon will promote periods of heavier snow showers across the mountains at times, but overall accumulations look to remain below advisory levels in the 2 to 5-inch range. Messy travel conditions may develop at pass level, especially late this afternoon into this evening. Exercise caution if traveling!
DRY WEATHER THROUGH MIDWEEK, POTENTIALLY ACTIVE AGAIN LATE WEEK:

Skies will clear by Tuesday morning with northerly flow behind the departing trough as a high pressure ridge moves in from the west. This will lead to dry conditions and much colder temperatures Tuesday night as efficient radiational cooling takes place. A weak shortwave trough looks to move through on Thanksgiving Day but QG forcing shows signs of splitting with not much impact to the area. With a large area of high pressure building off the SoCal coast and Desert Southwest, the northern stream looks to remain active with systems moving through the Pacific Northwest and Northern Rockies. This potentially keeps northwest flow across the area, potentially feeding moisture into the Park Range for favored orographics late this week into the coming weekend. There is some disagreement on how this evolves but potential exists for active weather during this timeframe with impacts particularly to the Park Range. Overall with ridging mid to late week, temperatures look to warm up to around 5 to 10 degrees above normal.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Upper ridge building across the Rockies will bring warmer and drier weather to the region Wed, then a weak upper trough and cold front drops temps back slightly on Thanksgiving day, though conditions will remain dry.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Scattered snow showers expected across the mountains/valleys today, with a few showers spilling onto the plains this evening and overnight.
- Any accumulating snowfall today/tonight looks light, with spotty 1-3 inches amounts over the mountains and generally less than an inch at lower elevations.
- Warmer and generally dry weather then expected through Thanksgiving, before a few snow showers return to the central mountains over the weekend.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Upper wave over the Great Basin early this morning will move toward CO today, then pass across the state overnight. System will bring snow showers to the Continental Divide this morning, with showers then spreading across most of the mountains/valleys during the afternoon. Precip in general looks rather light, with some spotty accums of 1-3 inches over the peaks and high passes by late day. Some weak instability (CAPE 50-150 J/KG) develops along the I-25 corridor and across the adjacent plains by late afternoon, suggesting that at least a few showers may make it onto lower elevations this evening, with CAMS pointing to the area from Walsenburg to La Junta as a location to watch. Overall, any snow amounts away from the mountains look patchy and light, though any stronger convective showers may snow hard enough to at least whiten the ground in spots for a brief period this evening. Surface/mid level low briefly strengthens overnight near the KS border as upper wave ejects into the plains, which may enhance snow showers over the far southeast into early Tue morning, and a few spots near the border could see at least some minor accums by sunrise Tue. System lifts into the central plains on Tue, with any lingering showers ending shortly after sunrise and skies clearing through the morning. Expect max temps both today and Tuesday to run near/slightly below seasonal averages, while overnight lows drop into the teens/20s at most locations.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Upper ridge building across the Rockies will bring warmer and drier weather to the region Wed, then a weak upper trough and cold front drops temps back slightly on Thanksgiving day, though conditions will remain dry. Ridge flattens and upper jet sags back southward toward CO over the weekend, though models differ on the timing of how quickly this happens. In any event, main feature of this pattern will be warm and increasingly breezy conditions from Friday onward, with potentially a few bouts of snow showers along the Continental Divide, mainly from Monarch Pass northward.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Beyond Thanksgiving, a more active pattern looks to return for the end of the forecast period and beyond.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Fairly quiet weather is forecast across the region through Thanksgiving with temperatures running near normal for the latter portion of November.
- A more active pattern will return next weekend with elevated chances for valley rain and mountain snow persisting into the following week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Relatively quiet weather is expected through Thanksgiving across the forecast area, with temperatures fluctuating within a couple degrees of normal for the latter portion of November. A couple of weak weather features will cross the region during this timeframe bringing increases in mid-high cloud cover, but little if any chance for measurable precipitation. The first system currently entering the Great Basin will progress eastward across the forecast area through Monday, with only a small chance of light precipitation mainly across the central Utah mountains. A second splitting wave will cross the region Wednesday bringing another increase in cloud cover but little else.

Beyond Thanksgiving, a more active pattern looks to return for the end of the forecast period and beyond. As early as Friday, a landfalling AR across the Pacific Northwest will spread moisture inland, with roughly 30% of models (heavily influenced by EC ensemble members) bringing this moisture into far northern Utah. Confidence is relatively high that a more progressive pattern with a series of shortwave troughs will become established later in the weekend into the following week, bringing an elevated chance for valley rain/mountain snow.

2660.travel_advice: Dangerous avalanche conditions. Careful snowpack evaluation, cautious route-finding and conservative decision-making essential.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: You can trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you on steep, shady leeward slopes at upper elevations. You could also trigger avalanches from a distance, so give suspect slopes a wide buffer.
Wind-drifted slabs sit over weak snow on shady slopes from west to north to east near and above treeline. Safer travel can be found on lower-angled slopes and in wind-sheltered areas below treeline.

2753.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Your chances of triggering an avalanche increase the higher you travel on the mountain, especially in previously wind-drifted areas. Use extra caution or simply avoid steeper slopes near and above treeline on northwest to north to east-facing slopes. There's a chance you could trigger a slope from a distance away, so be aware of other parties nearby.

2754.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Krista Beyer
bottom_line: Most slopes are generally safe from avalanches due to shallow or discontinuous snow cover. You might be able to trigger a small avalanche where recent winds have formed pockets of stiffened snow below ridgelines, on lee slopes, and around rocky outcrops in the alpine.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: Snow cover is still too thin for avalanches on most slopes. In the alpine, you should steer around hard drifts of snow on steep terrain features and below ridgetops. Unfortunately, the slopes with enough snow to ride are also where you might find enough snow for slides.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has begun to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. 6-12 inches of new snow has fallen between Friday the 13th and Monday the 16th. Another 6-12 inches could stack up by the end of the week. If you're traveling in the mountains this week, watch out for wind slabs 1-2 feet thick above 7,000 feet and pay attention to terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: From 60-degree temperatures to over a foot of new snow, the weather sure has changed quickly over the past week. A cooler and wetter weather pattern has taken shape over our region since Friday the 13th. As of Monday (16th) afternoon, some mountain locations have picked up 6-12 inches of new snow along with southerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH.
Wind Slabs
• Wind slabs could become reactive this week with over a foot of new snow and gusty winds. Wind slabs will be most sensitive just below ridgelines.
• Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices.
• Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
• Strong winds and local terrain features can alter the prevailing wind direction. Pay attention to cross-loading and wind-loading on unsuspecting slopes.
Early Season Conditions
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Check Your Winter Gear

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
Continuing Education
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with the winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
Observations
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: The snow cover is too thin for slides on most slopes, so avalanche danger is LOW. Recent snow drifts rest on weak, old snow. If you find a continuous drift of firm snow on a steep terrain feature, you can trigger a small slide. Steer around drifted pockets of snow where you see them below ridges or inside gullies.
